rationale: IPA affricate ligature withdrawn from official IPA; identical referent. Only Kyrgyz corpus uses ligature style.

No Turkic language in the set contrasts tap vs trill; one rhotic phoneme with positional allophones. Turkish/Azerbaijani corpora wrote ɾ; Kazakh/Kyrgyz/Uyghur/Uzbek wrote r. Merged to majority symbol r.
citation: Zimmer & Orgun 1999 (tr tap); Mokari & Werner 2017 (az tap); McCollum & Chen 2021 (kk trill reducing to tap); Ido 2025 (uz tap, final trill)

rationale: Turkish low vowel is acoustically central-to-back; JIPA writes /a/ by convention. All other languages incl. Finnish use ɑ for the cognate vowel. Small real fronting in Turkish accepted as loss.
citation: Zimmer & Orgun 1999; Kopkallı-Yavuz acoustics; McCollum & Chen 2021

rationale: Uzbek lost vowel harmony (Iranian contact); its a/ɔ low system is a different phonological object, not the front/back harmonic pair. Do NOT merge uz a with ɑ.
Uzbek orthographic o = /ɔ/ ranging [ɑ]~[ɔ̝]; phonemically distinct from a. Keep.
Kazakh ы genuinely centralized to schwa-like [ə]; not a respelling of ɯ.
Kazakh і = [ɪ]; genuine Kipchak high-vowel reduction.
Kazakh ө = [ɵ]; part of the same reduced system.
Uvular stop is a genuine inventory feature absent in Turkish/Azerbaijani(written)/Finnish. Handled by assimilation table (q->k for tr listeners) not by merging.
citation: McCollum & Chen 2021; loanword adaptation studies (Arabic loans in Turkish)

rationale: Phonemic /ae/ in Azerbaijani (9-vowel) and Uyghur; true inventory difference vs Kyrgyz/Turkish.
Kyrgyz has phonemic long vowels (historical contraction); Uzbek ː only in Arabo-Persian loans. Keep where produced.
Arabic punctuation in Uyghur corpus; punctuation not phonology.

Uyghur corpus prefixes many words with ʔ (e.g. ʔbiri); pipeline-added initial glottal stop absent from every other corpus and from McCollum 2021 transcriptions -> systematically inflated Uyghur distances. Stripped. Reversible if team objects.

Ido 2025 transcribes Uzbek affricates as alveolo-palatal t͡ɕ/d͡ʑ/ɕ but notes [t͡ʃ]/[d͡ʒ]/[ʃ]-like realizations are common inter-/intra-speaker variants. Corpus t͡ʃ/ʃ convention kept as defensible; documented for methods section.
